endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: In addition, identify how recalls/corrections will be managed and ascertain whether there is a defined process and threshold for reporting potential patient harm.

commentary.bottom_line: No study in this evidence map tests whether a defined recall, correction, and harm-reporting process with a risk threshold shortens the time harmful AI stays in use, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation currently rests on a single framework endorsement from the CHAI Responsible AI Guide.

perspectives.view: The map contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single supporting source is a consensus framework, which reflects expert judgment rather than measured outcomes.

The CHAI Responsible AI Guide asks organizations to identify how recalls and corrections will be managed and whether a defined process and threshold exist for reporting potential patient harm. This is a voluntary framework statement worded as a should, and the supplied sources do not tie it to any binding requirement.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare organizations with and without a defined AI recall and harm-reporting process. They should measure time from first harm signal to withdrawal or correction, the number of patients exposed during that interval, and the rate of reported harms. Descriptive work documenting how often harmful AI tools remain deployed after problems surface would also establish the size of the hazard, which the map currently lacks.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence exists for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot yet tell whether harm-reporting thresholds would detect problems that fall mainly on these groups, whose harms may be underreported through standard channels.
